title: Should investors take a bite of Apple? - News - Sarasota Herald-Tribune - Wiredfocus
text:
Should investors take a bite of Apple? – News – Sarasota Herald-Tribune August 27, 2018
You could say that Apple Corp. (AAPL), the first U.S. stock with a $1 trillion market capitalization, has had a good year. When I wrote about it last year, it was selling for about $160. It was recently about $218, a gain of 36 percent. With such a substantial gain, it’s timely to review its prospects for the next five years, since some of that gain may have been “borrowed” from the future.
Currently, most published analysts are extremely bullish on Apple. That’s not surprising, as iPhone sales have been better than expected and a new model may be on sale soon.
Let’s review recent quantitative data and see what my model says about its price by September 2023, the end of that fiscal year.
• Apple is rated “B” for growth and “C” for value by Zack’s.
• Its average earnings forecast is $13.56 a share for fiscal year 2019 and 11.68 for 2018.
• Its published longer-term earnings-growth rate forecasts range from 10 to 13 percent.
• Its price-to-earnings ratio based on 2019 forecasted earnings and its recent $218 price is 16.1 and is below the market’s.
• Its current dividend yield is $2.92 (about 1.4 percent).
• AAPL has recently had about twice the volatility of the S&P 500.
Based on data like this, my statistically based model draws the following conclusions about fiscal year 2023.
It forecasts that the chances are 1 out of 2 that the price will be higher than $339, 2 out of 3 that it will be between $320 and $359, and 1 out of 100 that it will be less than $232.
The statistical model deals with complications, such as different views of future earnings, to provide quantitative forecasts.
Based on the model’s forecast, what rate of return might an investor reasonably expect over this period?
Based on the $320 price, investors can forecast about a 7.8 percent compound annualized appreciation. To this should be added the dividend for a probable compound annualized total return of at least 9.2 percent.
Given its volatility, are these returns large enough to justify investments in Apple?
It depends on what other opportunities are available. For example, I estimate the compound annual total return of the less volatile and diversified S&P 500 is going to be around 6 percent for that period.
There are uncertainties. Apple’s gross profit margin is about 38 percent. Analysts expect it to be stable. If it rises, for example, due to the introduction of some new products, the stock’s price would benefit. If it falls, the stock’s price would be hurt. Longer-term, any substantial stock price increase depends on Apple’s ability to deliver longer-term double-digit earnings growth. A single-digit growth rate will disappoint investors and limit the stock’s appreciation.
In summary: Apple stock’s returns are likely to be good but not as “eye-popping” as the last two years.
Before any final decision, investors should review Apple’s balance sheet and 10-Q and 10-K filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission. These can be found at secfilings.com.
